name: Julie Renee Carlson
justification: For us, I’d put not using an AI story device first for now. Nora is five, and I’d want to understand what limits and privacy protections are in place before she could use one on her own. That doesn’t mean I’d never try it with her. If I did, C would be a relatively inexpensive way to try it, and the pictures might make the stories more engaging for her. E is next: I like the audio-only idea, though I’d still have questions about a young child using the app independently. D is a simpler, screen-free option, but at the price of a low-end tablet it feels like a lot to pay for one function. A is last for me because it combines that higher price with a screen. I’d be more comfortable trying any of these together first than treating independent use as a reason to buy.

name: Yusuf Bennett
justification: As described, I’d pass for now. I’m not comfortable assuming that “no parent supervision needed” means the stories are always appropriate or that a young child’s conversations aren’t being stored. If those basics were clear and I could use it with Sami, A would be my first choice among the devices: it’s limited to storytelling, and the pictures are useful at his age. It’s expensive, though. C is a much cheaper way to try the idea, but I wouldn’t want him opening an app on a phone or tablet any time without me around. D avoids the screen, but costs as much as a low-end tablet for audio alone. E is cheap, but has the same app-access concern and no illustrations.

name: Ethan Christopher Doyle
justification: I wouldn’t buy any of these for Owen to use independently as described, at least not without understanding the content safeguards and what information the service collects. For occasional use together, E is the easiest to consider: it’s audio-only and just $10, though I’d want to know what setup or account it needs. D has the advantage of being a dedicated audio-only device, but at the price of a low-end tablet, that’s a lot for one purpose. C is inexpensive, but I don’t think the images add enough to make me prefer a screen for this. A costs much more and adds a screen, so it’s the least appealing to me. I’d still want to be there with him rather than treating any of these as a replacement for reading together.

name: Martin Joseph Zielinski
justification: At four, I would not buy an open-ended AI storyteller for Eli to use on his own without knowing more about content safeguards and privacy. “No supervision needed” doesn't mean I have to leave him unsupervised, but I wouldn't use that as the plan. If I did try one together with him, C is a low-cost way to see whether he actually enjoys it, and the pictures could give us something to talk about. E is also inexpensive and avoids adding images, though it still means using our phone or tablet. A has the advantage of being single-purpose, but tablet-level money is a lot for a device like this. D costs the same and gives us audio only, so I see less reason to buy it. At home, a regular book and reading together are still the sure thing.

name: Molly Grace Hartwell
justification: I’d rather not use an AI storyteller for a 3- to 5-year-old unless I knew more about how it handles a child’s requests and what safeguards or privacy protections are in place. “No supervision needed” doesn’t mean a parent can’t be nearby, but I wouldn’t assume it’s something I’d let a four-year-old use on her own. If I did try one, E is the least expensive way to start, and audio-only avoids adding more screen time. D has the benefit of being a single-purpose device without a screen, but the low-end-phone price is a lot for one function. C is inexpensive, but the screen and access to an existing phone make it less appealing. A combines a screen with the higher device cost, so it would be my last choice.

name: Kelsey Morgan Pritchard
justification: I’d put no AI device first for now, mostly because I’d want clearer information about privacy and how the stories are kept age-appropriate. If I did try one, the $10 app with pictures seems the easiest to test, and illustrations matter for this age. The audio-only app is next; it costs the same and keeps the screen out of the story, though Nora enjoys looking at pictures. I’d put the dedicated devices lower because they cost as much as a low-end tablet, which feels like a lot for something we haven’t tried. Between those, I’d pick the one with illustrations over audio-only. I might use any of them with me close by at first, even if supervision isn’t required.

name: Tiana Rochelle Baptiste
justification: I’d be most willing to try the inexpensive audio-only app, as long as I could keep the phone and use it with my child rather than make it an unsupervised thing. C is next because pictures can make a story fun to look at together, though I’d be mindful of adding screen time. D has the advantage of being just a storyteller and no screen, but that’s a lot more money for something I haven’t tried. A has pictures too, but I’d have the same cost concern and would rather not add another screen device. B is last because I’m open to seeing a sample and trying something new—but I wouldn’t take “no supervision needed” to mean I’d actually leave a 3-to-5-year-old alone with it.

name: Kaylee Annabelle Prescott
justification: I’d put no AI device first because I already like reading books with my daughter, and I’m not sure I want her making up stories with AI on her own. If I tried one, E seems like the least expensive way to see if she even likes it, though I’d want to be with her while she uses it. I’d put C next: the pictures could be fun, but audio is enough for a story and I don’t really want to add screen time just for that. D avoids the screen, but a whole device that costs as much as a low-end phone is hard to justify. A is last for me because it has that same device cost plus a screen. The idea is interesting; I just wouldn’t treat “no supervision needed” as a reason to leave a preschooler using it alone.

name: Hannah Minji Choi
